items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: my Uncle Willie Santiago was one of the first guitar players of jazz, working with like Buddy Bolden

ctx.x: Your family is musical I know. Does it go back a ways?

Oh yeah. Well it goes back actually my Uncle Willie Santiago was one of the first guitar players of jazz, working with like Buddy Bolden and like Bunk Johnson and people way, way back. Because my mother’s family, her father’s family was from Santiago, Chile. And they had come to New Orleans to perform and decided to stay there. I guess it was a heck of a trek to get to New Orleans from Chile in — this was about 1873 or something like that. I mean so then after the gig is over you’ve got to go back. I don’t know…
No way — they went to New Orleans to just play?

items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Because I had an old uncle who played with Buddy Bolden

ctx.x: Well I don’t actually know that much about it. But it was kind of like where, kind of slaves and people of color or whatever you want to call them kind of celebrated their rituals and parties or jazz festivals or whatever they wanted to call it in that day you know? And that’s where a lot of that stuff was developed. And it was not too influenced

by anything else but what was in New Orleans, because New Orleans was pretty isolated. That’s the way I see it. You read these books and you know, people go off to the moon and different things, and you know everyone’s got a story. But that’s the way I see it. I mean I’m a fourth generation New Orleanean so I feel pretty good about saying that. Because I had an old uncle who played with Buddy Bolden, and so I’m a fourth generation musician also. And New Orleans is just a really special place in the world. I…
And it isn’t just the people. For instance, the whole sensational palette is enlivened. The food.
